reason: Attacked and not broken. Translation drift is the obvious line of attack on a French letter, so I did not take the verifier's reading on trust: I downloaded the named translation myself, Project Gutenberg 5115, and read letter CCCI in full. The title page is decisive on the translator: Gutenberg's own metadata reads 'Translator: Aimée L. McKenzie' and the text's title page reads 'The George Sand-Gustave Flaubert Letters / Translated by A.L. McKenzie (1921)', so translator and year in the source are confirmed from the book and not from a secondary citation. The letter's heading reads 'CCCI. TO GEORGE SAND / December, 1875', which confirms number, addressee and date. The paragraphs run: 'Your good letter of the 18th, so maternally tender, has made me reflect a great deal', then 'I am constantly doing all that I can to enlarge my brain', then the quoted sentence, so 'third paragraph' is right, and the card's source claims no paragraph at all, only the letter. McKenzie prints: 'I do not enjoy making “desolation,” believe me, but I cannot change my eyes!' The card reads word for word the same; the only difference is that the printed double quotation marks around desolation become the house curly singles, with the comma still inside, which is the house punctuation rule and not a change of wording. Nothing is minted and nothing is paraphrased. I also checked the verifier's account of why the word is in quotation marks at all, since a false gloss in an evidence field is worth catching: Sand's preceding letter, CCC to Gustave Flaubert, reads 'What's our next move? For you, of course, DESOLATION, and, for me, consolation', so Flaubert is quoting her word back at her. That is accurate. Attribution: the letter is Flaubert's, in a volume of the two writers' correspondence, so there is no reporter-versus-speaker trap; Flaubert appears on the misattribution list only through a travel line the Calendar carries ('Travel makes one modest'), which is nothing to do with this and is not what is proposed. Scope: an 1875 letter in a 1921 translation, not scripture, film, lyric, proverb, business or oratory, well before 1999, nothing needing a content warning. shipped.js: shipped [], near [], person 'gustave flaubert' yearCount 0, not banned, not at cap; no second Flaubert among the month's sixty-one proposals or the June carry-ins. Mechanics: the source leads with the name, has no dash, no straight double quote, and runs 134 characters, inside the 140 cap, with the translation in parentheses as the rule asks; the quotation is prose, unbroken, and ends in an exclamation mark; tag Correspondence is the form of the work. Theme and hour: a man telling a friend he cannot trade away how he sees is plain speech about clarity, and it is rueful rather than bleak. One soft spot, not a refutation: the note field is empty, so a reader meets ‘desolation’ in quotation marks with nothing to say whose word it is. One line saying he is quoting Sand's own word back to her would make the card legible on its own.
